The lighthouse keeper, Elias, had spent thirty years tending the beacon on the jagged cliffs of Cape Morrow. His days were measured not in hours but in the rhythm of the sea, the creak of the great lens, and the silence that pressed against the glass of the watch room. He was a man of few words, and the only conversation he ever had was with the gulls that circled above the tower.

One October morning, the tide had pulled back further than usual, exposing a stretch of black rock that Elias had never seen before. There, wedged between two stones, he found a glass bottle, its cork swollen with salt and age. Inside, a piece of paper was rolled tight, unmarked by the water.

He carried it up the spiral stairs, his old knees aching, and set it on the workbench beside his ledger of records. He had kept a ledger for decades, noting the weather, the ships that passed, and the strange things the sea delivered to his shore. Each entry had a number and a code, just like the ones he had seen in the old maritime archives.

He unwrapped the paper with trembling fingers. The message was short, written in a faded ink that had survived the years in the bottle.
